title: Multivariable & Vector Calculus
subject: Calculus
summary: Vectors and coordinates in 3D, partial derivatives and optimisation, multiple integrals with Jacobians, line and surface integrals, and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss. Built around the calculus of electromagnetism and thermodynamics, with explicit chemistry hooks (exact differentials, Maxwell relations, Boltzmann via Lagrange, orbital volume elements).

units.title: Vectors, Coordinates, and Curves in Space
units.summary: Parametric curves, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, vector algebra in 3D (dot and cross products, lines and planes), and vector-valued functions for motion; the geometric language of every physics course after this one.

lessons.title: Parametric curves and polar coordinates
objectives: Parametrise a curve (line, circle, ellipse, cycloid, helix projection) and eliminate the parameter when possible.
Compute dy/dx and d^2y/dx^2 for a parametric curve and the arc length integral of sqrt(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2).
Convert between polar and Cartesian coordinates, sketch r = f(theta) for standard curves, and compute the area enclosed, (1/2) integral r^2 d theta.
Write the arc length in polar form and the slope of a polar curve.
Identify conic sections in polar form r = ed/(1 + e cos theta) and relate eccentricity to orbit shape.

lessons.title: Vectors in 3D: dot product, cross product, and triple products
objectives: Perform vector addition, scaling and decomposition into components in 3D, and compute magnitudes and unit vectors.
Compute the dot product, the angle between vectors, and the scalar and vector projections; interpret W = F . d.
Compute the cross product by determinant and by the right-hand rule, and interpret |a x b| as parallelogram area and the torque tau = r x F.
Evaluate the scalar triple product a . (b x c) as a volume and as a determinant, and state when three vectors are coplanar.
Use index notation with the Kronecker delta and Levi-Civita symbol to verify a . (b x c) = b . (c x a) and the BAC-CAB rule.

lessons.title: Lines, planes, quadric surfaces, and cylindrical and spherical coordinates
objectives: Write parametric, vector and symmetric equations of a line in 3D and the equation of a plane from a point and a normal vector.
Find the angle between planes, the distance from a point to a plane, and the intersection of a line and a plane.
Identify and sketch quadric surfaces (ellipsoid, hyperboloid, paraboloid, cone, cylinder) from their equations using traces.
Convert between Cartesian, cylindrical (r, theta, z), and spherical (rho, theta, phi) coordinates, stating the physics convention for theta and phi.
Describe a region such as a sphere, cone, or cylinder in the most convenient coordinate system, e.g. an atomic orbital's volume element.

lessons.title: Vector-valued functions: velocity, acceleration, arc length, and curvature
objectives: Differentiate and integrate vector-valued functions r(t) component-wise and state the product rules for dot and cross products.
Compute the tangent vector T, speed, and arc length of a space curve, and parametrise by arc length.
Compute curvature kappa = |dT/ds| and decompose acceleration into tangential and normal components.
Derive the constancy of the angular momentum direction for a central force from r x p and show that r x r-dot = const implies motion in a plane (Kepler's second law).
Describe the helix as a model for a charged particle in a magnetic field with r(t) = (R cos wt, R sin wt, vz t).

units.title: Partial Derivatives and Optimisation
units.summary: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, the total differential and chain rule, the gradient and directional derivative, and constrained optimisation with Lagrange multipliers; the calculus of thermodynamics (exact differentials, Maxwell relations) and of the Boltzmann distribution.

lessons.title: Functions of several variables and partial derivatives
objectives: Describe a function of two or three variables with level curves, level surfaces and cross-sections, e.g. isotherms of P(V, T) or a potential-energy surface.
Compute partial derivatives, including higher-order and mixed partials, and state Clairaut's theorem that the mixed partials are equal for smooth functions.
Interpret a partial derivative with its held-fixed variables made explicit, e.g. (dU/dT) at constant V versus at constant P.
Define limits and continuity in several variables and show a limit fails to exist by comparing two paths.
Check whether a function satisfies a PDE such as Laplace's equation by computing second partials.

lessons.title: Tangent planes, the total differential, and the chain rule
objectives: Find the equation of the tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at a point and use it as a linear approximation.
Write the total differential df = f_x dx + f_y dy and use it to propagate errors in a function of several measured variables.
Apply the chain rule to compositions with several intermediate variables, drawing a dependency tree.
Differentiate implicitly using F(x, y, z) = 0, dz/dx = -F_x/F_z, and verify the triple-product (reciprocity) relation (dx/dy)_z (dy/dz)_x (dz/dx)_y = -1 on the ideal gas law.
State and apply the Leibniz rule for differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter.
keyEquations: \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)_z\left(\frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\right)_x\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)_y=-1

lessons.title: The gradient and directional derivatives
objectives: Compute the gradient of a scalar field in Cartesian coordinates and state that it is perpendicular to level sets.
Compute the directional derivative D_u f = grad f . u and find the direction of steepest ascent and its rate.
Find the tangent plane to a level surface F(x, y, z) = c using the gradient as normal.
Compute the force F = -grad V from a potential energy and verify with a 2D example such as a harmonic or Coulomb potential.
Relate the gradient to the total differential, df = grad f . dr.
keyEquations: \nabla f=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right)

lessons.title: Optimisation and Lagrange multipliers
objectives: Find critical points of f(x, y) and classify them with the second-derivative (Hessian) test, including saddles.
Find global extrema on a closed region by checking the interior and the boundary.
Apply Lagrange multipliers to extremise f subject to g = c, and interpret lambda as the sensitivity of the optimum to the constraint.
Derive the Boltzmann distribution by maximising entropy -sum p_i ln p_i subject to sum p_i = 1 and sum p_i E_i = <E> using Lagrange multipliers (chemistry hook).
Fit a line by least squares by minimising the sum of squared residuals as a function of the two parameters.

units.title: Multiple Integrals
units.summary: Double and triple integrals in Cartesian, polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, centres of mass and moments of inertia (rotational spectroscopy), and change of variables with Jacobians (volume elements for orbitals and phase space).

lessons.title: Double integrals: rectangular regions, general regions, and polar coordinates
objectives: Define the double integral as a limit of Riemann sums and compute it as an iterated integral over rectangles (Fubini's theorem).
Set up and evaluate a double integral over a type I or type II region and exchange the order of integration.
Convert a double integral to polar coordinates with dA = r dr d theta and evaluate it.
Evaluate the Gaussian integral integral e^(-x^2) dx = sqrt(pi) by squaring it and switching to polar coordinates.
Compute areas, volumes under surfaces, and averages of functions over regions.

lessons.title: Triple integrals in rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates
objectives: Set up triple integrals over solid regions in Cartesian coordinates and sketch the region.
Use the volume elements dV = r dr d theta dz (cylindrical) and dV = rho^2 sin phi d rho d phi d theta (spherical) and choose the coordinate system from the symmetry.
Evaluate the volume of a sphere, a cone and a spherical cap by triple integrals.
Integrate a radial function over all space, e.g. the normalisation of a hydrogen 1s density |psi|^2 = e^(-2r/a)/(pi a^3), and state the radial probability density 4 pi r^2 |psi|^2.
Compute the average of a function over a sphere and explain why the average of a harmonic function equals its centre value (stated, proved later).

objectives: Compute the mass and centre of mass of a lamina or solid with a variable density by double or triple integrals.
Compute the moment of inertia of a disc, rod, and sphere about an axis through the centre, and verify using the parallel-axis theorem.
Compute the inertia tensor components of a simple rigid body or molecule and relate the principal moments to rotational constants B = hbar^2 / 2I in spectroscopy.
Compute the gravitational (or electrostatic) force/potential at a point from a uniform spherical shell and conclude the shell theorem.

objectives: Compute the Jacobian determinant of a coordinate transformation and explain its geometric meaning as an area or volume scale factor.
Derive the polar, cylindrical and spherical volume elements as Jacobians.
Change variables in a double integral to simplify the region or the integrand (e.g. u = x + y, v = x - y over a parallelogram).
Use scale factors h_i to write dV = h1 h2 h3 du dv dw in orthogonal curvilinear coordinates.

units.title: Vector Fields and Line Integrals
units.summary: Vector fields, line integrals and work, conservative fields and potentials (path independence and exact differentials in thermodynamics), and Green's theorem.

lessons.title: Vector fields and line integrals
objectives: Sketch a 2D vector field from its components and identify sources, sinks and circulation by eye.
Compute line integrals of scalar functions with respect to arc length and of vector fields (work) over a parametrised path.
Evaluate the line integral of F . dr for a field along a straight segment, circle and general curve and note the effect of reversing orientation.
Express work done by a variable force as a line integral; distinguish a closed-path integral from an open one.

lessons.title: Conservative fields, potentials, and exact differentials
objectives: State the equivalent conditions for a conservative field: path independence, zero circulation on closed loops, F = grad f, and curl F = 0 on a simply connected domain.
Test a 2D field with the condition P_y = Q_x and find a potential function by integrating.
Apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals W = f(B) - f(A).
Decide whether a differential M dx + N dy is exact; connect this to state functions: dU and dS are exact, dq and dw are not.
Derive a Maxwell relation from the equality of mixed partial derivatives of a thermodynamic potential (chemistry hook).

lessons.title: Green's theorem

Evaluate a line integral around a closed curve by converting to a double integral, and vice versa.
Use Green's theorem to compute the area of a region as (1/2) closed integral (x dy - y dx).
Extend Green's theorem to regions with holes, and explain why the circulation of a curl-free field can be nonzero when the domain is not simply connected (the 1/r angular field).
Explain the 2D curl as the circulation per unit area and 2D divergence as flux per unit area.

units.title: Divergence, Curl, and the Integral Theorems
units.summary: Divergence and curl, surface integrals and flux, Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem; the mathematics in which Maxwell's equations and the conservation laws are written.

lessons.title: Divergence and curl
objectives: Compute the divergence and curl of a vector field in Cartesian coordinates and interpret them as local expansion (sources) and local rotation.
Compute the Laplacian of a scalar field and check Laplace's equation for 1/r in 3D.
Verify that the curl of a gradient and the divergence of a curl are zero, and state why this makes a conservative field irrotational.
Determine from a picture whether a field has non-zero divergence or curl at a point.
Recognise div and curl as the operators in Maxwell's equations and the continuity equation d(rho)/dt + div J = 0.
keyEquations: \nabla\cdot\vec F=\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}

Compute the flux of a vector field through a surface using the area element for a graph, a sphere, or a cylinder.

lessons.title: Stokes' theorem
objectives: State Stokes' theorem and the right-hand-rule orientation relating the surface normal and the boundary direction.
Evaluate a closed line integral as a surface integral of the curl, and vice versa, choosing the easier surface.
Explain why the surface integral of a curl depends only on the boundary curve (surface independence) and relate this to div(curl F) = 0.
Derive Faraday's law (integral form) from the differential form curl E = -dB/dt using Stokes' theorem.
Show that Green's theorem is the planar special case of Stokes' theorem.

Derive the integral form of Gauss's law from the differential form div E = rho / epsilon0 and the integral form of a continuity equation.
Explain what goes wrong when a field has a singularity inside (the 1/r^2 field) and handle it by excising a small sphere.

units.title: Vector Identities, Curvilinear Operators, and Physics Applications
units.summary: Vector-calculus identities, the gradient, divergence, curl and Laplacian in cylindrical and spherical coordinates, and a workshop on applying the theorems to electromagnetism, gravity and transport; the bridge into P2, P5 and M5.

lessons.title: Vector identities and operators in curvilinear coordinates
objectives: Use the del operator and index notation to prove the product rules, e.g. div(fA), curl(fA), div(A x B), and grad(A . B).
Prove curl(curl A) = grad(div A) - nabla^2 A and use it to derive the wave equation for E in vacuum.
Write the gradient, divergence, curl and Laplacian in cylindrical and spherical coordinates using scale factors, and quote them for use later.
Compute the Laplacian of a radial function f(r) in spherical coordinates and solve nabla^2 f = 0 for r > 0.
Use the identities to simplify a calculation instead of expanding in components.
